lines.t: Let us go through your preparation for Thursday's mock trial. Elena, you represent the prosecution, and Marcus, you are for the defence. Where are you now?
I have the case file. Our defendant is accused of stealing a bicycle from the rack outside the engineering building.
And our case is that he was in the library at the time.
Marcus, what evidence do you have for that?
The library entry system records that his card was used at seven fifty and again at nine ten. The theft happened at about eight forty.
Good. Elena, who will you call as witnesses?
First, the owner of the bicycle, to explain what was stolen and how much it was worth.
Second, the security guard, who saw someone in a grey jacket near the rack. I also wanted to call the cleaner, who found the broken lock.
How long is the trial? We have only forty minutes in total.
Then I will leave out the cleaner. Two witnesses are enough.
Wise. Remember, you must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The burden is on you, Elena, not on Marcus.
So my job is to create doubt. The guard was thirty metres away, it was dark, and the camera footage is blurred.
Exactly, and you can raise that in cross-examination. There you may ask leading questions, such as, is it true that the light was poor?
But you may only ask questions. Do not make speeches.
Understood. How long are the opening statements?
Three minutes each. Keep them simple. Tell the jury what you will prove, and do not argue yet.
Who is on the jury?
Six classmates. Their names will be drawn from a hat. They will not have read the case file, so explain everything clearly.
Where and when is the trial?
Thursday at two o'clock in Room Four of the law building. Arrive fifteen minutes early to set up the room.
Should we wear formal clothes?
Yes, please. Jackets or smart shirts. It helps you take the role seriously.

lines.t: Noor, thanks for sending your list of ideas. Let us talk them through. You have three options, correct?
Yes. First, whistleblower protection laws. Second, corruption risks in public procurement. And third, using artificial intelligence to detect fraud in public spending.
What attracts you to the third one?
Honestly, it connects my master's with the doctorate I want to do later. But I am worried about the data.
You are right to worry. Many governments publish spending data only in summary form, and a thesis needs detailed records.
Without them you would spend months searching rather than analysing.
What about whistleblower laws? There is a lot written on that.
That is the problem. It is a crowded field.
You would have to find something new to say, and examiners will expect you to compare several countries, which takes time.
So procurement looks like the middle path?
It could be. There are open contract databases, and some include three years of detailed records.
You could look for warning signs, such as contracts awarded with only one bidder.
Could I still use some AI there?
In a small way, yes. Simple statistical tools could highlight unusual contracts. But I would not promise too much.
Remember, the thesis is only twelve thousand words, and you have eight months.
Right. How narrow should I go?
Very narrow. Perhaps one sector, such as road construction, in one region. A narrow study done well is better than a broad one done badly.
That makes sense. Initially, I thought of including hospitals as well.
Leave hospitals for the doctorate. Now, what do you need to do next?
Write a one-page outline with my research question and the data source.
Exactly. Please also ask the librarian about access to the contract database, because some sites need a university login and approval can take several days.
Send the outline within three weeks. Let us meet next Wednesday at ten to check your progress.
Thank you, Dr Kemp. I feel much clearer now.

o: The data is easy to find

lines.t: Good morning. Today I want to explain how human memory works, and why some study methods work far better than others.
Psychologists usually divide memory into three stages. The first is encoding, when information enters the brain.
The second is storage, and the third is retrieval, when we bring it back.
Let us begin with short-term memory. For decades, textbooks said it holds about seven items.
More recent research suggests the real figure is closer to four, if we count meaningful chunks.
What is a chunk? Think of a phone number. If you try to remember eleven separate digits, you will probably fail.
But if you group them into three or four blocks, the task becomes much easier.
Information in short-term memory fades after roughly twenty seconds unless we repeat it or connect it to something we already know. Connection is the key idea here.
A fact attached to an existing memory is much more likely to survive.
Long-term memory, by contrast, seems to have no practical limit. The challenge is not storage but retrieval.
You may know a name perfectly well and still fail to recall it, because you lack the right cue.
Cues can be surprising. Smell is a famous example. Many people report that the scent of a certain soap suddenly brings back a whole childhood afternoon.
Now, forgetting. In the 1880s, a German psychologist tested himself on lists of nonsense syllables.
He found that forgetting is fastest soon after learning: most of the material was lost within the first day.
This is why cramming the night before an exam is unwise. A better method is spaced repetition.
Review the material after one day, then after a week, then after a month, and each review will make the memory stronger.
Sleep also matters. During sleep, the brain replays the day's experiences and moves important information into long-term storage.
Students who sleep well after studying usually remember more than those who stay up all night.
Finally, a practical tip. Many students re-read their notes again and again, but this gives a false feeling of knowing.
Testing yourself with questions is much more effective, even if it feels harder.
So, to summarise, use chunks, create connections, space your reviews, sleep well, and test yourself. Thank you.

lines.t: Good afternoon. Today's lecture is about the design of cities, and about one simple question: who is a city built for?
For most of history, cities grew without a master plan. Medieval towns developed around a market or a river crossing, and their streets were narrow and winding.
This looks chaotic on a map, but it has advantages.
In hot climates, narrow lanes create shade, and old city centres in many countries are still pleasant to walk in during summer.
Planned cities are also very old. Ancient builders often used a grid, with straight streets crossing at right angles.
A grid is easy to build, easy to measure, and easy to navigate, which is why many cities in the nineteenth century copied it.
The biggest change came in the twentieth century with the car. Planners introduced zoning, which means separating areas by purpose.
Homes went in one zone, offices in another, and shops in a third. Highways connected them.
The result was long commutes. In some cities, workers spend more than an hour travelling each way.
Traffic jams, noise and air pollution followed, and streets stopped being places where people met and became channels for vehicles.
Today many designers are trying to reverse this trend. A popular idea is the fifteen-minute city.
In it, most daily needs, such as school, shops, a clinic and a park, are within fifteen minutes on foot or by bicycle.
To achieve this, planners promote mixed-use buildings, for example apartments above a bakery and a small office. They also convert car lanes into cycle paths and wider pavements.
Green space is another priority. Trees and parks make a city cooler in summer, because shade and evaporation can lower local temperatures by several degrees.
They also improve mental health and give children somewhere safe to play.
Of course, there are criticisms. First, rebuilding an existing city is very expensive.
Second, when a neighbourhood becomes more attractive, prices often rise, and poorer residents may be forced to leave. This is called gentrification.
So what lessons can we draw? Firstly, good design puts people before vehicles. Secondly, good design must also protect the people who already live there.
Next week, we will look at a case study of a city that tried to do both.
Thank you, and please read chapter five before then.

title: A short history of courts and written law

lines.t: Today I want to give you a short history of courts and written law, and to explain why writing the law down was such an important step.
Before writing, rules existed as custom, memorised and passed on by elders. The problem is obvious.
Memory changes, and powerful people can claim that the custom says whatever suits them.
Some of the earliest written laws come from Mesopotamia, about four thousand years ago.
One famous collection was carved on a tall stone pillar and placed in a public place, so that people could see what the rules were.
Many of its provisions set fixed penalties, which limited private revenge.
A similar idea appears in ancient Rome. Around four hundred and fifty years before the modern era, Roman citizens demanded that the law be displayed in the forum.
The result was known as the Twelve Tables.
Much later, in the sixth century, the emperor Justinian ordered scholars to collect and organise Roman law into a single code, and that work influenced European legal thinking for centuries.
Now let us move to medieval England. After the Norman conquest, royal judges began to travel around the country to hear cases.
When they met, they compared decisions, and over time the rulings became a shared body of rules.
This is the origin of common law, which relies heavily on precedent, meaning earlier decisions in similar cases.
England also developed the jury, a group of ordinary citizens who decide the facts.
In 1215, a charter forced on the king stated that no free man could be imprisoned without a lawful judgment.
This was not a modern bill of rights, but it established that even rulers were bound by law.
Meanwhile, much of continental Europe followed the Roman tradition. In 1804, France published a civil code, written clearly so that ordinary people could read it.
This approach, called civil law, puts the main rules in written codes, and judges apply them rather than building on earlier cases.
Today these two traditions have moved closer together. Common law countries have many statutes, and civil law courts also pay attention to earlier decisions.
Why does this matter? Three features run through this history: laws that are written, laws that are public, and courts that give reasons.
Together, they make it hard for officials to act in secret, which is why they are central to the fight against corruption.
In the next lecture, we will look at how judges are appointed. Thank you.
